analysis.one_liner: Removes dollar caps on compensatory and punitive damages in workplace discrimination lawsuits.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate committee where it was referred, and Congress ended without a floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the Civil Rights Act of 1991, workers who win intentional employment discrimination cases can recover only a capped amount of compensatory and punitive damages, with caps ranging from $50,000 to $300,000 depending on the employer's size; race discrimination claims under a different statute have no caps. This bill would strike those caps entirely, letting juries award whatever compensatory and punitive damages the facts support, and would clarify that any party in such a case may demand a jury trial. It was referred to the Senate labor committee and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who suffer intentional discrimination based on race, sex, religion, disability, or national origin. If the bill passed, a jury could award damages up to the full amount of their losses—including emotional distress—and punitive damages, instead of being limited to the statutory caps. Workers bringing claims under other civil rights statutes, which already have no caps, would no longer see discrimination victims treated differently depending on which law they sue under.

how_it_helps.text: Strikes the paragraph of 42 U.S.C. 1981a that caps the compensatory and punitive damages available in intentional employment discrimination cases, so awards would no longer be limited to amounts between $50,000 and $300,000 by employer size.
Amends the jury trial provision so that any party to a discrimination case may demand a jury trial, which affects who decides the damages award.

The bill's stated purpose is to equalize remedies available to all victims of intentional employment discrimination, ending the gap between capped Title VII-style claims and uncapped claims under other statutes.

analysis.who_pays: Employers found liable for intentional discrimination—large corporations and small businesses alike—would face uncapped jury awards for compensatory losses and punitive damages, increasing their liability exposure and settlement values in these cases. Insurers and employers' legal defense costs would rise accordingly.

drawbacks.text: Without caps, jury awards for compensatory and punitive damages can be large and unpredictable, and small businesses in particular face potentially ruinous exposure; this is the trade-off an honest supporter acknowledges—the uncertainty is the point, because uncapped liability is what deters discrimination.

The bill addresses only damages for intentional discrimination claims under the specified federal provisions; it does not change who can sue or what conduct counts as discrimination, so its effect is limited to the size of awards in cases victims already win.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers, the benefit is real: full compensation for proven harm and punitive awards that deter intentional discrimination, ending a system where the same injury pays differently depending on the statute. The cost falls on employers as greater, less predictable liability, some of which lands on small businesses that face the same uncapped exposure as large corporations. The core trade-off is deliberate—uncapped damages are meant to make discrimination expensive—but the bill offers no accommodation for smaller employers.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate labor committee, which never took it up, and the 105th Congress ended with the bill still sitting there.

narrative.text: Senator Kennedy of Massachusetts introduced the bill on April 7, 1997, joined by 13 Democratic cosponsors, all senators.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources on the day it was introduced.
No further action appears in the record—no hearings, no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote—before the Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers facing discrimination lawsuits are better off, because the caps on compensatory and punitive damages—$50,000 to $300,000 depending on employer size—remained in place, limiting their exposure; discrimination victims gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers, whose damage caps stayed in place

for.name: Sen. Edward M. Kennedy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Equal Remedies Act of 1997 to remove damages caps in employment discrimination cases.

for.name: 13 Senate Democratic cosponsors
for.role: Senators including Leahy, Dodd, Harkin, Boxer, Wellstone, Feingold, and Mikulski
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; no Republican senator signed on.

against.name: Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction (chair: Sen. James Jeffords, R-VT)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no recorded action—no hearing, no markup, no vote—for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: No Republican cosponsored the bill, and the Republican-controlled Senate never scheduled it for floor consideration.

sides.party_line_note: All 14 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, with no Republican support in the record, and the bill died in committee under a Republican-led Senate; no roll-call vote was ever taken.

industries.industry: Employers (all industries with 15 or more employees)
industries.note: The bill would have made employers liable for uncapped compensatory and punitive damages when juries find intentional discrimination. Its interest in keeping the caps runs against workers' full compensation for proven harm.

industries.industry: Employment litigation insurers and defense bar
industries.note: Uncapped awards raise settlement values and exposure, increasing insurance costs and defense spending for employers facing discrimination suits.
